title: Why is There a Battle Over Net Neutrality?
summary: Josh and Chuck explain net neutrality: the principle that internet service providers must treat all lawful traffic equally, without fast lanes, slow lanes, blocking, or throttling. They trace its roots in common carrier telephone regulation, the FCC's back-and-forth classification of ISPs as telecom versus information services, the 2010 and 2015 Open Internet Orders, and the 2017 push under FCC chairman Ajit Pai to roll back Title II reclassification via "Restoring Internet Freedom." They cover arguments for and against, including infrastructure investment, paid prioritization, peering disputes between Netflix and Comcast and Verizon, and the Verizon-Yahoo Tumblr and Flickr account issue. The episode opens with tour dates and closes with a listener mail about the Stonewall episode.

segments.title: Tour dates announcement
segments.summary: Hosts announce 2017 tour dates in Toronto, Chicago, Vancouver, Minneapolis, Austin, Lawrence, Kansas City, Brooklyn, and Atlanta, with ticket info at sysk live dot com.

segments.title: Intro and framing the episode
segments.summary: Hosts explain the episode is a substitute for going dark for Battle for the Net Action Day, and define net neutrality as an open internet with no fast or slow lanes.

segments.title: Net neutrality basics and public opinion
segments.summary: Explanation of how the open internet let Facebook launch without negotiating with ISPs, the role of ISPs as last-mile providers, and polling showing broad support including among conservatives. The debate centers on how to achieve neutrality, through FCC policing or competition.

segments.title: Corporate split and 2015 FCC rules
segments.summary: The dispute is between ISPs such as Verizon, Comcast, and AT&T and tech companies such as YouTube, Netflix, Facebook, and Google. The 2015 FCC rules barred blocking, throttling, and fast lanes. Trump later appointed Ajit Pai, who opposes those rules.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Short break before the historical section.

segments.title: History: telephone common carriers and dial-up
segments.summary: Telephone companies were treated as common carriers. The FCC in the 1970s and 1980s guaranteed the right to attach modems, and later required lines be opened to DSL providers. The telecom versus information services distinction was drawn.

segments.title: Classification fights from Bush to Wheeler
segments.summary: The Bush-era FCC classified ISPs as information services after a court ruling. Rules under Genachowski in 2010 were struck down after Verizon challenged them. Tom Wheeler's weaker 2014 proposal drew backlash, then he issued the 2015 Open Internet Order reclassifying broadband as Title II telecommunications.

segments.title: Ajit Pai, light-touch regulation, and rural infrastructure
segments.summary: Pai, a former Verizon lawyer, favors light-touch regulation and argues that deregulation would encourage rural broadband investment. Hosts discuss the Universal Service Fund as a funding model and the debate over whether harms are hypothetical.

segments.title: Infrastructure investment data and legal argument
segments.summary: Lobby group US Telecom reports a drop in ISP infrastructure spending after reclassification, while the US Census Bureau reports an increase. The Administrative Procedure Act's bar on capricious rule changes makes this data central to the legal fight.

segments.title: Break and comment call-to-action
segments.summary: Break, then hosts ask listeners to comment on the FCC proceeding 17-108 Restoring Internet Freedom, and recall John Oliver's 2014 segment that crashed the FCC site.

segments.title: Arguments for and against, and paid peering
segments.summary: Arguments for net neutrality include preventing ISP censorship and protecting startups. Arguments against include infrastructure investment risk and ISPs becoming content providers, such as Verizon's Yahoo acquisition affecting Tumblr and Flickr. Netflix and Comcast and Verizon peering dispute is discussed, along with paid prioritization.

segments.title: Closing debate on trust and regulation
segments.summary: Hosts argue that unregulated markets tend toward greed harming consumers, and that the core question is whether ISPs can be trusted to act fairly. They encourage FCC comments through August 6.

segments.title: Listener mail: Stonewall episode
segments.summary: A listener named Craig praises the Remembering Stonewall episode, and the hosts share contact information.

segments.title: Outro
segments.summary: Sign-off with contact and website information.
